newsitem.title: TURKEY: FEATURE - Politics casts shadow over Turkish economy.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Politics casts shadow over Turkish economy.

text.p: Turkey's fast-growing economy is crying out for structural reforms but the government is too concerned with political battles to tackle problems endangering long-term economic stability.
The sprawling social security system and inefficient tax collection fed a budget deficit of around 10 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) last year.

Some analysts believe the economy is overheating as the current account deficit swells. They fear a repeat of 1994's crisis when GDP shrank six percent. Political tensions are also a factor, scaring foreign investors and increasing the cost of borrowing for Turkish banks.

"The macroeconomic situation is not very encouraging, and if the economy keeps growing too fast, the current account deficit may become unfinancible," said David Lubin, emerging markets analyst at HSBC in London.
Confirming investors fears, Moody's downgraded its rating of Turkey's debt and currency to B1 from Ba3, citing both fiscal and political concerns.
ATMOSPHERE OF ECONOMIC CRISIS

"Since 1994 there has been an atmosphere of crisis and this has not been put to rest," said Bahar Sahin, general secretary of the Istanbul Chamber of Industry. "What the government call reforms are populist measures to save the day and lack long-term vision," she said.

The government of Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan inherited in 1996 an economy growing around seven percent and likely to expand five percent annually in coming years. But accompanying this is persistent annual inflation of 80 percent, yawning current account and fiscal deficits and an unwieldy social security system.

"Turkey could actually have a very bright future but it is a country which does not exploit its potential. There must be reform throughout the state system to capitalise on its assets," Abdurrahman Yildirim, an economy columnist at the liberal daily Yeni Yuzyil told Reuters.

He said the country needs a gommitted to widening the tax base and reforming the loss-making public sector. "And one which will close the major wound to the budget presented by the social security institution (SSK)."
The SSK is expected to have a debt of $10 billion by 2000 if measures such as raising the pension age are not taken.

Revenue-raising plans proposed by the eight-month-old government, such as accelerating a sluggish privatisation programme, have been welcomed by financial markets, even though critics say this is a one-off solution.
Stocks have surged 50 percent this year and public debt maturities lengthened to 14 months from six. Yields have fallen to around 95 percent from more than 130 percent last year.

The government has programmed a balanced budget for 1997, hoping to earn billions of dollars from privatisation, and pledged a medium-term programme to create single-digit inflation within three years. Analysts are sceptical about these targets.
LONG-TERM STABILITY SEEMS ELUSIVE

A recent row between Erbakan's Welfare Party and the military-dominated National Security Council over the apparent Islamisation of the secular state has helped erode confidence in the government and many analysts doubt the coalition has a long-term future.
Concern about the political outlook and Welfare's Islamist agenda has added to the doubts of foreign investors.
"Among potential foreign investors there is uncertainty about the political situation and uneasiness about Welfare," said Ercan Uygur, a professor of economics at Ankara University.
Some foreign analysts believe the Welfare Party may manage to introduce some measure of stability into the economy because otherwise it will find it impossible to pursue its political agenda.
But in such a case, short-term economic stability would turn into increased long-term political risk as Welfare's plans clashed with strong secular elements, including the powerful army.
"Even if there is short-term stability, long-term there is going to be instability because the relations between Welfare and the establishment can only be antagonistic," HSBC's Lubin said.

Foreign investor reticence casts doubt on the government's target of raising $5 billion from privatisation in 1997, Uygur said. A recent sale tender for state steel maker Erdemir only drew two bids, reinforcing doubts about investor demand.
Foreign investment inflow into Turkey declined by more than 30 percent last year despite optimism over a 1996 customs agreement with the European Union.
But MUSIAD, a leading association of Moslem businessmen, says the international concerns about Welfare are misplaced.
"There is an erroneous perception of the Welfare Party. It is one of the leading parties in encouraging foreign investment," said MUSIAD deputy chairman Ali Bayramoglu.
DEBT SERVICING, CURRENT ACCOUNT
The Treasury and public institutions are expected to service around $8 billion of foreign debt this year, compared to fresh borrowing on international markets of at least $2 billion.

Turkey's foreign debt rose by end-September to $78.04 billion from $73.28 billion at the end of 1995 and $65.60 billion at end-1994. Political uncertainty, combined with doubts on the government's economic plans have made foreign borrowing The current account situation has worsened, chiefly because of a rise in the trade deficit due to the adverse effects of the customs union with the EU and the relatively slow rate of Turkish lira devaluation. The current account showed a $2.31 billion deficit in the first half of 1996 and is expected to show a deficit of $6.9 billion in the full year, compared with a deficit of $2.34 billion in 1995 and a surplus of $2.63 billion in 1994.
BANKERS URGE IMF ACCORD
International Monetary Fund officials are due to visit Turkey in April for talks which are seen as vital to restoring foreign confidence in the economy.

Turkish officials are not seeking funds, but would welcome a sign of support from the IMF. The Fund urges Turkey to implement a comprehensive anti-inflationary plan and has expressed doubts about the government's economic targets.
Local bankers have urged the government to reach a new stand-by accord with the IMF. A previous plan put in place after the financial crisis in 1994, was abandoned after 17 months.
EU NOT HELPFUL SHUNNING STRONGER TIES WITH TURKEY
On the political front, relations with the European Union have been soured by senior EU politicians who have cast doubt on Turkey ever achieving full membership.
Expectations of an export boom resulting from the customs union have been disappointed by a 32 percent jump in Turkey's EU trade deficit to $804 million in the first half of 1996.

MUSIAD's Bayramoglu said that while Turkey still sought full EU membership it would not force the issue if European opposition continued. Instead it would consider its other trade options internationally.
"Turkey must maintain its links with Europe but it must also look to develop links in the Far East, the United States and Africa," he said.

Reflecting this outlook, Erbakan led a trade tour of Moslem countries soon after coming to power last June and sealed a $23 billion gas supply accord with Iran which has since drawn criticism from the United States.
Turkey rejects criticism of its trade policy and points to sharply rising energy supply and the United Nations embargo on Iraq which Turkey says has cost it $27 billion in lost trade since 1991.
The EU's attitude has been criticised by local and international analysts alike on the grounds that it made the life of pro-Western forces in the country more difficult.

"A sense of rejection by the EU can make it more easy for Islamic influence to grow," said Lubin. "The most sensible thing to do would be to promote economic integration, while evading the membership issue."
